CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 22




           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

         IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                  )
         OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                    )
         FOR AN ORDER OF THE COMMISSION                       )
         APPROVING ITS NEW EXTRA LARGE LOAD                   )
         TARIFF AND TERMS AND CONDITIONS OF                   )   CASE NO. PUD2026-000046
         SERVICE FOR EXTRA LARGE LOAD                         )
         CUSTOMERS AND A REGULATORY ASSET TO                  )
         RECOVER COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH                        )
         PORTFOLIO OPTIMIZATION SOFTWARE                      )




                                            Direct Testimony

                                                    of

                                            Kimber L. Shoop

                                               on behalf of

                                   Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company




                                              June 17, 2026
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 2 OF 22




                                                 Kimber L. Shoop
                                                 Direct Testimony

    1   Q.     Please state your name and business address.
    2   A.     My name is Kimber L. Shoop. My business address is 321 North Harvey, Oklahoma City,
    3          Oklahoma 73102.
    4
    5   Q.     By whom are you employed and in what capacity?
    6   A.     I am employed by Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (“OG&E” or “Company”) as the
    7          Director of Regulatory Affairs.
    8
    9   Q.     Please summarize your educational background and professional qualifications.
   10   A.     I earned a Bachelor of Arts degree in Government from the University of Virginia (1996)
   11          and a Juris Doctorate from the University of Oklahoma College of Law (2002). I am a
   12          member of the Oklahoma Bar Association, the Arkansas Bar Association, and the District
   13          of Columbia Bar Association. After law school, I practiced law in Washington D.C. until
   14          accepting the position of Senior Attorney at OG&E in 2006. In 2015, I was named
   15          Managing Director of Law at OG&E. In 2017, I left OG&E to establish a private law
   16          practice in Edmond, Oklahoma and continued to perform work for OG&E. In 2020, I
   17          returned to OG&E as Director of Regulatory Policy and Planning before being named
   18          Director of Regulatory Affairs in 2022.
   19
   20   Q.     What is the purpose of your testimony in this proceeding?
   21   A.     The purpose of my testimony is to provide an overview of OG&E’s request for
   22          Commission approval of a new Extra Large Power and Light (“XLPL”) tariff for certain
   23          large load customers, as required by Final Order No. 753440 in Case No. PUD2025-
   24          000038, and consistent with the requirements of Oklahoma House Bill 2992 (“HB 2992”),
   25          which goes into effect July 1, 2026. I will also provide the results of OG&E’s portfolio
   26          optimization software cost and benefit study, which was also required by Final Order No.
   27          753440. In addition, I will introduce the other witnesses presenting testimony on behalf of
   28          OG&E in this proceeding and provide a broad overview of the proposed tariff structure.

        Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                  Page 2 of 16
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 3 OF 22




    1
    2   Q.     What other OG&E witnesses are sponsoring testimony in this proceeding?
    3   A.     In addition to my testimony, Gwin Cash, OG&E’s Senior Manager of Pricing, Rate
    4          Administration, and Load Analysis is filing Direct Testimony to explain both the XLPL
    5          tariff and accompanying Terms and Conditions of Service for Extra Large Customers
    6          (“T&CXLLC”) in detail. Also, Matthew DeCourcey, Vice President in the Energy Practice
    7          at Charles River Associates, is providing Direct Testimony which explains how OG&E’s
    8          XLPL tariff compares to other large load tariffs and contracts around the country.
    9
   10   Q.     Does this filing satisfy the requirements in Final Order No. 753440 issued in Case No.
   11          PUD2025-000038?
   12   A.     Yes. This filing satisfies the requirements of Commission Order No. 753440, which directs
   13          OG&E to seek approval of a new large load tariff by July 1, 2026. OG&E is proposing the
   14          XLPL tariff to comply with that requirement and to set a standard for how OG&E can serve
   15          large load customers while ensuring all other customers are protected. Also, the Oklahoma
   16          Legislature recently passed HB 2992, which goes into effect July 1, 2026. This filing also
   17          addresses the requirements of HB 2992 to “establish and maintain separate terms and
   18          conditions of electric service applicable to any large load customer” and to “create and
   19          maintain separate tariffs applicable to such large load customers.” 1
   20
   21   Q.     What is OG&E’s intent in crafting the XLPL Tariff and the accompanying
   22          T&CXLLC?
   23   A.     OG&E recognizes the prospect of adding new large loads to the grid has raised concerns
   24          from existing customers and policy makers regarding how these large loads will impact
   25          customer rates. OG&E proposes the XLPL tariff and T&CXLLC in order to address these
   26          concerns. As this Commission is aware, OG&E wants to grow and serve new businesses,
   27          but it also wants to maintain affordable rates and reliability for all customers. While OG&E
   28          seeks to attract new businesses, the Company also needs to make sure its current customers
   29          are protected and OG&E grows its system responsibly.

        1
               17 Okla. Stat. §903 (effective July 1, 2026).
        Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                   Page 3 of 16
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 4 OF 22




    1                 First, it is worth noting at the outset that adding these large loads will benefit
    2          OG&E’s existing customer classes by paying their allocated portion of all existing shared
    3          system costs. Put simply, the additional large load customers with increased usage help
    4          pay the existing costs of the entire system and reduce the average cost to serve each
    5          customer. Existing system costs will be spread over many more kilowatt-hours, resulting
    6          in all retail customers on the system paying less per kilowatt-hour. The new loads,
    7          therefore, put downward pressure on rates for all customer classes, including residential,
    8          commercial, and industrial customers. For example, in Case No. PUD 2026-000031,
    9          OG&E witness Jason Thenmadathil testified about the clear benefit to existing customers
   10          of adding Google’s load to OG&E’s existing cost of service study.
   11                 As this Commission is aware, however, to serve any new large loads, additional
   12          costs will be incurred. OG&E seeks to establish necessary terms and conditions of service
   13          for these large load customers that protect other customer classes from rate increases that
   14          could be caused by these additional investments. These customer protections contained in
   15          the XLPL tariff and the T&CXLLC will be discussed in detail by OG&E witness Gwin
   16          Cash. Such provisions include:
   17                 •       Contribution in aid of construction (“CIAC”) payments for all transmission
   18                         and distribution infrastructure associated with serving the customer’s new
   19                         or expanded load, ensuring large load customers pay all such costs
   20                         associated with delivering power and connecting to the grid.
   21                 •       Significant performance security to ensure fulfillment of the financial
   22                         obligations arising from the Company providing service to the new large
   23                         loads, which protects customers from rate increases.
   24                 •       Required long-term commitments from these large load customers with fees
   25                         imposed on those large load customers should they leave the OG&E system
   26                         or reduce their demand prior to the end of the contract term.
   27                 •       Minimum demand and energy charges to ensure large load customers pay a
   28                         minimum amount regardless of actual usage and a fair share of costs
   29                         incurred to serve the large loads.


        Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                   Page 4 of 16
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 5 OF 22




    1                 •       A “Customer Class Protection Charge” will be charged to XLPL customers
    2                         if an adverse impact on other customer classes is demonstrated after
    3                         considering additional costs of providing service to those extra-large load
    4                         customers. This charge will be reviewed and addressed in each general rate
    5                         proceeding.
    6                 •       Creation of a new Customer Affordability Charge for extra-large load
    7                         customers that will be credited to residential customers to offset increasing
    8                         rates.
    9
   10   Q.     Please explain the process OG&E undertook to develop the proposed XLPL Tariff
   11          prior to filing this case.
   12   A.     Prior to filing this case, OG&E engaged in many negotiations with Google, which
   13          ultimately resulted in an executed special contract to provide electric service for three new
   14          datacenter projects. That contract provided the foundational regulatory framework within
   15          which the XLPL tariff and the accompanying T&CXLLC were developed.                       The
   16          development of the tariff was also informed by the requirements of HB 2992, which will
   17          become effective on July 1, 2026 and will be codified as Sections 901 through 905 of Title
   18          17 of the Oklahoma Statutes. HB 2992 mandates that all electric suppliers establish and
   19          maintain separate terms, conditions, and tariffs applicable to large load customers,
   20          including credit requirements and other measures necessary to ensure that such customers
   21          reimburse the electric supplier for all costs fairly allocated to them, and that the term of
   22          service for a large load customer be at least ten years.
   23                 In developing the specific provisions of the proposed tariff and T&CXLLC, OG&E
   24          also drew upon the work of Matthew DeCourcey, whose testimony in this proceeding
   25          provides a comparative analysis of large load tariffs and contracts offered by other utilities
   26          around the country, ensuring the protections and structural features incorporated into the
   27          XLPL tariff are informed by and consistent with emerging industry practice for serving
   28          customers of this scale.




        Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                    Page 5 of 16
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 6 OF 22




    1   Q.     What threshold or criteria would require a customer to take service under the
    2          proposed XLPL tariff?
    3   A.     As set forth in the T&CXLLC , a customer is required to take service under the XLPL tariff
    4          if it meets the definition of any one of three customer types. Customer Type 1 encompasses
    5          any customer beginning service with OG&E after July 1, 2026, and expected to have an
    6          annual peak demand of 75 MW or more. Customer Type 2 encompasses existing customers
    7          taking service before July 1, 2026, whose future billing demand is expected to either
    8          increase by 75 MW or more above their billing demand prior to July 1, 2026, or increases
    9          its demand and has a total demand of 125 MW or more. Customer Type 3 encompasses
   10          existing customers taking service before July 1, 2026, who may not be adding load, but
   11          whose service conditions change in such a manner that OG&E would be required to add
   12          generating capacity to meet a 75 MW or higher increase in demand for that existing
   13          customer.
   14
   15   Q.     Why did OG&E create three different types of customers that would take service
   16          under the XLPL Tariff and T&CXLLC?
   17   A.     These different types of customers were identified to ensure any customer (existing or new)
   18          that causes OG&E to have a new service obligation of 75 MW or more should be subject
   19          to the customer protections contained in the XLPL tariff and T&CXLLC. This means a
   20          brand new customer with load of 75 MW or higher or an existing customer who adds at
   21          least 75MW or grows to 125 MW or more will become subject to the XLPL Tariff and
   22          T&CXLLC.
   23
   24   Q.     Can you explain why OG&E has a Customer Type 3 and the difference between Type
   25          3 and the other types of customers?
   26   A.     There could be certain situations where an existing customer may not add load but still
   27          require OG&E to add 75 MW or more of generating capacity. For example, this could be
   28          necessary if a customer no longer participates in or no longer qualifies for OG&E’s Load
   29          Reduction Program. Additionally, as this Commission is aware, the Southwest Power Pool
   30          rules around how utilities count Load Reduction is evolving. OG&E wants to ensure any

        Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                  Page 6 of 16
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 22




    1          existing customer that causes OG&E to add an increase in generating capacity also falls
    2          under the XLPL tariff and T&CXLLC. If OG&E needs to add 75 MW or more capacity
    3          for a large load customer, the customer protections afforded by the XLPL tariff and
    4          T&CXLLC should apply.
    5
    6   Q.     Why did OG&E select 75 MW as the load requirement for the XLPL Tariff and
    7          T&CXLLC?
    8   A.     This is the megawatt value contained in HB 2992 (17 Okla. Stat. §901(4)). Originally,
    9          OG&E was considering a 100 MW threshold for large load customers to be captured by
   10          the XLPL tariff and T&CXLLC, but changed it to 75 MW after the passage of HB 2992.
   11
   12   Q.     Please describe the customer protections contained within the XLPL tariff and the
   13          T&CXLLC.
   14   A.     The proposed XLPL tariff and the accompanying T&CXLLC incorporate a comprehensive
   15          set of customer protections that operate at multiple levels to safeguard OG&E’s existing
   16          customers from potential cost shifts associated with serving large load customers, while
   17          also establishing structural protections for OG&E itself against financial exposure from
   18          customer default or early departure. As discussed in detail in the testimony of OG&E
   19          witness Cash, these protections include a 15-year minimum service term with termination
   20          and capacity reduction fees, a CIAC requirement, a collateral requirement, special pricing
   21          provisions, minimum billing demand and energy obligations, and a reservation charge
   22          mechanism. Rather than repeat the full explanation of each provision provided in Mr.
   23          Cash’s testimony, I will briefly summarize the function of each protection as a matter of
   24          policy overview and explain why each of these customer protections are important.
   25
   26   Q.     Please summarize the requirement for a long-term commitment for large load
   27          customers taking service under the XLPL tariff.
   28   A.     The 15-year minimum service term following the load ramp-up period, combined with the
   29          termination and capacity reduction fees defined in the Electric Service Agreement
   30          (“ESA”), protects existing customers from stranded cost risk by ensuring OG&E has

        Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                 Page 7 of 16
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 8 OF 22




    1          contractual certainty over a duration sufficient to recover the capital investments made to
    2          serve the XLPL customer.
    3
    4   Q.     Are there customer protections in case an XLPL customer terminates early or reduces
    5          its capacity during the term?
    6   A.     Yes. In order to protect other customers from losing the benefits of the large loads and
    7          avoid having to pay for stranded costs that could be incurred in this situation, OG&E’s
    8          T&CXLLC includes fees if an XLPL customer terminates the contract or reduces its
    9          contract demand during the term. First, such a termination or capacity reduction can only
   10          occur after the ninth year and the XLPL customer must give a three-year notice. This
   11          means any termination or capacity reduction can only occur after the 12th year of the term.
   12          Second, in the case of a capacity reduction, the XLPL customer can only reduce its contract
   13          demand by a maximum of 25 percent. Third, if an XLPL customer terminates or reduces
   14          its contract demand, it will be required to prepay one hundred percent (100%) of the
   15          Minimum Charges for the remainder of the initial contract term impacted by such early
   16          termination or capacity reduction in the form of a one-time fee in order to make any such
   17          election effective. Because an XLPL customer cannot provide the requisite three-year
   18          notice for termination or capacity reduction until year 9, the amount of Minimum Charges
   19          associated with any early termination exit fee or capacity reduction fee will not exceed
   20          three (3) years of Minimum Charges. The ESA contained in the T&CXLLC also provides
   21          that in no event shall any early termination exit fee or capacity reduction fee be less than
   22          one year of Minimum Charges.
   23
   24   Q.     What is a CIAC and why is it necessary for large load customers?
   25   A.     A CIAC is payment from a customer to the utility to cover costs of utility infrastructure.
   26          Any CIAC received from a customer allows the utility to make the infrastructure
   27          investment without adding it to rate base and without earning a return on the investment or
   28          otherwise including the investment in rates. In the T&CXLLC, the XLPL customer would
   29          be required to pay a CIAC reflecting all transmission and distribution infrastructure costs
   30          associated with serving its new or expanded load (plus applicable taxes). This means

        Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                   Page 8 of 16
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 9 OF 22




    1          transmission and distribution infrastructure costs specific to serving these customers are
    2          not included in OG&E rates and therefore are not recovered over time through the payment
    3          of rates.
    4
    5   Q.     Can you explain the benefits of the collateral requirement?
    6   A.     The collateral requirement obligates XLPL customers to provide credit support covering
    7          100 percent of the minimum charges for 60 months of the initial term of the ESA in the
    8          form of cash, an irrevocable standby letter of credit, or a guaranty meeting specified credit
    9          rating thresholds, protecting OG&E and its existing customers from the financial exposure
   10          that would result if an XLPL customer were to default on its payment obligations. OG&E
   11          recognizes that not all XLPL customers may be able to shoulder a collateral requirement
   12          that consists of 100 percent of minimum charges through the full course of the initial term.
   13          Therefore, the T&CXLLC requires collateral covering 100 percent of the minimum charges
   14          for just sixty (60) months of the Initial Term.
   15
   16   Q.     What special pricing provisions are OG&E proposing for large load customers?
   17   A.     There are two special pricing provisions that will apply to XLPL customers through the
   18          XLPL tariff. The Customer Class Protection Charge is a tariff-embedded capacity charge,
   19          initially set at $0.00 per kW per month, that may be established or adjusted in future general
   20          rate cases, subject to Commission approval. The Customer Class Protection Charge
   21          provides the Commission with a recurring, structured opportunity to assess whether the
   22          XLPL class is causing costs to be borne by other customer classes and, if so, the ability to
   23          set the charge at a level sufficient to remedy any impact.
   24                  In addition, the tariff includes the Customer Affordability Charge of $2.50 per kW
   25          per month assessed on Billing Demand which generates revenues that are placed in a
   26          regulatory liability to be credited to residential customers, providing an affirmative
   27          financial benefit to residential customers as a direct result of XLPL service.




        Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                     Page 9 of 16
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 10 OF 22




    1   Q.     Do the Customer Class Protection Charge and the Customer Affordability Charge
    2          serve different purposes?
    3   A.     Yes. The Customer Class Protection Charge ensures other customer classes are held
    4          harmless from any demonstrated adverse impacts of serving the XLPL customers, while
    5          the Customer Affordability Charge provides separate, guaranteed benefits to residential
    6          customers independent of whether any adverse rate impacts occur.
    7
    8   Q.     Can you explain in more detail OG&E’s decision to include the Customer Class
    9          Protection Charge?
   10   A.     This is a customer protection initially negotiated and included in OG&E’s recent ESAs
   11          with Google and OG&E incorporated this concept into the XLPL Tariff as a specific charge
   12          for all XLPL customers. As described by OG&E witness Thenmadathil in Case No.
   13          PUD2026-000031 as a “fail-safe,” he testified that it recognizes there is the potential for
   14          adverse rate impacts to other customer classes due to future costs of serving the XLPL
   15          customers. He further testified there are clear rate benefits from adding XLPL loads and
   16          shifting shared system costs from other customer classes to the XLPL class due to the
   17          nature of their large contribution of kilowatt-hour consumption. However, if the costs of
   18          serving those XLPL customers ends up outweighing those “cost shift” benefits, this
   19          Customer Class Protection Charge exists for OG&E and the Commission to remedy any
   20          such adverse impacts.
   21
   22   Q.     How would OG&E calculate the Customer Class Protection Charge?
   23   A.     As discussed by OG&E witness Thenmadathil in Case No. PUD2026-000031, OG&E
   24          would perform and submit a separate Cost of Service Study (“COSS”) in future rate cases,
   25          which tests whether serving XLPL customers (including Google) had an adverse rate
   26          impact on other customer classes. The demonstrative analysis would essentially be a COSS
   27          with and without the XLPL load and a proportional share of the XLPL load’s contributing
   28          generation need, essentially providing a “what if” scenario of what rates would be if the
   29          XLPL customers were not customers on the system. If there is an adverse impact on other



        Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                 Page 10 of 16
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 11 OF 22




    1          customer classes, the adverse impacts would be used to create a $/KW-month charge and
    2          that revenue would be credited back to other customer classes.
    3
    4    Q.    Why is OG&E proposing a Customer Affordability Charge?
    5    A.    Whereas the Customer Class Protection Charge is meant to hold other customer classes
    6          harmless in the case of costs to those customer classes outweighing the benefits, the
    7          Customer Affordability Charge is designed to create clear benefits for residential
    8          customers. This charge will go directly to a regulatory liability to be credited to residential
    9          customers.
   10
   11    Q.    How was the Customer Affordability Charge calculated?
   12    A.    As testified by OG&E witness Cash, OG&E designed the Customer Affordability Charge
   13          to collect approximately $30 million per year from 1,000 MW of load. This amount is the
   14          approximate total of the Company’s LIAP program, an expanded Senior Discount for all
   15          residential customers who qualify as senior citizens, and approximately 20 percent of our
   16          residential energy efficiency program.
   17
   18    Q.    How much benefit will the Customer Affordability Charge provide to residential
   19          customers?
   20    A.    With just a single 1,000 MW XLPL customer, the Customer Affordability Charge will
   21          generate more than $400 million over the life of a 15-year agreement, for the benefit of
   22          residential customers. Any amount collected through this charge would be placed into a
   23          regulatory liability and provided to residential customers after each rate proceeding.
   24
   25    Q.    What additional provisions of the XLPL Tariff would you like to highlight that
   26          provide protections to customers?
   27    A.    The XLPL tariff contains billing minimums (both demand and energy) designed to ensure
   28          XLPL customers pay a minimum amount for the capacity and energy they request. In order
   29          to protect all other customers from stranded costs in the event an XLPL customer’s load is
   30          less than what the XLPL customer requests OG&E to plan for, the XLPL customer would

         Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                   Page 11 of 16
         Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 12 OF 22




    1          be required to pay a certain monthly minimum charge regardless of the energy consumed
    2          or capacity needed in a given monthly period. The XLPL tariff is set such that the billing
    3          demand will never be less than 85 percent of the contract demand corresponding to the
    4          monthly billing cycle, and the minimum billing energy is calculated using a 90 percent load
    5          factor requirement applied to the billing demand. The billed energy will be the greater of
    6          this calculated minimum energy and actual measured energy.
    7                 The minimum billing demand floor of 85 percent of the customer’s contract demand
    8          for the applicable billing month, combined with the minimum billing energy obligations,
    9          ensures OG&E recovers the fixed costs it incurs to serve an XLPL customer even if the
   10          customer’s actual measured demand or energy consumption falls below the contracted
   11          level in a given month.
   12
   13   Q.     What is a reservation charge and why is it considered a customer protection?
   14   A.     The reservation charge mechanism requires new XLPL customers who execute a
   15          Preliminary Agreement or ESA to pay a monthly charge calculated by multiplying the
   16          Customer Affordability Charge by the Maximum Contract Demand. This charge will be
   17          imposed for a maximum period of 24 months prior to the commencement of service.
   18          OG&E will not retain these revenues. Rather, the revenues collected from the Reservation
   19          Charge will be placed in the same regulatory liability as the Customer Affordability Charge,
   20          ensuring residential customers receive a financial benefit during the period between
   21          contract execution and the date the XLPL customer begins taking service. Since OG&E
   22          may incur costs to serve them before they come on-line, OG&E believes a reservation
   23          charge (based on the Customer Affordability Charge discussed above) is reasonable.
   24
   25   Q.     Is OG&E providing a Cost and Benefit Study on the use of Portfolio Optimization
   26          Modeling Software?
   27   A.     Yes. As required by Final Order No. 753440 in Case No. PUD2025-000038, OG&E has
   28          conducted a cost and benefit study of portfolio optimization modeling software and is filing
   29          the study as Direct Exhibit KLS-1 attached to my testimony.



        Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                 Page 12 of 16
        Case No. PUD2026-000046
 CASE PUD PUD2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 2 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 06/17/2026 - PAGE 13 OF 22




    1   Q.     What are the results of OG&E’s cost and benefit study?
    2   A.     OG&E’s cost and benefit study concludes that portfolio optimization software can provide
    3          meaningful benefits in both the Integrated Resource Planning and Request for Proposals
    4          contexts by systematically identifying least-cost resource portfolios, quantifying portfolio
    5          performance across a wide range of future scenarios, revealing cost drivers and binding
    6          constraints, and highlighting where incremental reliability or emissions benefits require
    7          material cost tradeoffs.
    8                  As shown in Direct Exhibit KLS-1, OG&E’s preliminary annual cost estimate for
    9          commercially available portfolio optimization software is up to $500,000, inclusive of user
   10          access, storage, vendor-provided data, initial training, and user support. The Commission
   11          should be aware that the study also identifies important limitations of such software, noting
   12          that portfolio optimization tools have limited ability to quantify or mitigate factors such as
   13          project development risk, execution complexity, contract terms, and counterparty
   14          considerations, which require separate commercial and due diligence review, and that
   15          differences in system architecture, workflow, transparency mechanisms, or runtime
   16          performance among available platforms may not translate into materially different
   17          portfolio selection outcomes. On balance, OG&E is supportive of the usage of a portfolio
   18          optimization tool in its evaluation of projects, while acknowledging that the qualitative
   19          factors noted above fall outside the scope of what such a tool can meaningfully evaluate.
   20
   21   Q.     How is OG&E proposing to handle the increased cost of the portfolio optimization
   22          software?
   23   A.     OG&E is proposing to recover the increased cost of the portfolio optimization software
   24          through a regulatory asset. OG&E proposes that any costs associated with the integration
   25          of portfolio optimization software be added to a regulatory asset, to be reviewed in a future
   26          rate case.




        Direct Testimony of Kimber L. Shoop                                                   Page 13 of 16
        Case No. PUD2026-000046

        Cost and Benefit Study of Portfolio
        Optimization Modeling
        1.    Introduction
        As part of the ﬁnal order in Case No. PUD 2025-00038, OG&E has been directed by the
        Oklahoma Corporation Commission (“Commission”) to conduct a cost/beneﬁt study of
        portfolio optimization modeling so that the Commission may evaluate the potential
        beneﬁts of such modeling before the Company’s next triennial integrated resource plan.


        2.    Methodology for resource selection
        Oklahoma’s Integrated Resource Planning (“IRP”) rules are detailed in Oklahoma
        Administrative Code (“OAC”) Oklahoma Corporation Commission’s (“OCC”) Electric Utility
        Rules OAC 165:35-37. IRPs must provide the Commission and stakeholders with updates
        on planning assumptions and risk factors. The IRP also establishes the need for future
        generation or capacity procurement. OG&E is required to ﬁle an IRP every three (3) years
        and ﬁle interim updates when material changes in planning assumptions occur. OG&E’s
        2026 IRP, submitted as an update, forecasts a need for incremental generation capacity
        primarily due to continued expansion of the Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”) Resource
        Adequacy framework and continued strength in regional demand trends.

        The subchapter 165:35-37-1-b (9) requires the IRP to establish the appropriate portfolio of
        products to be obtained through competitive procurement. Consistent with this
        subchapter, OG&E’s IRP process evaluates possible resource options and provides its
        preferred portfolio.

        The IRP analysis of resource options presents the results of detailed analysis associated
        with a range of technologies, the timing and availability of resources, and technology-
        speciﬁc risk factors. OG&E’s production cost modeling forecasts future operating margins
        by incorporating individual generating unit operating characteristics, transmission grid
        topology and constraints, unit commitment/operating conditions, and market system
        operations to model the SPP IM. Individual resource performance is then modeled across
        multiple sensitivities such as low gas and high gas costs, implementation of a CO2 tax, low
        and high solar costs as well as scenarios such as low and high fuel supply, and energy
        evolution across 30 years to calculate the 30-year Net Present Value of Customer Cost
        (“NPVCC”) under a wide range of future potential market conditions. The NPVCC differs

        for each resource due to the unique capital costs, O&M expenses, market revenues, tax
        incentives, in-service dates, and other factors.

        NPVCC modeling is a robust method of economically evaluating resources in an IRP
        setting. However, the NPVCC does not account for a variety of qualitative conditions and
        risks, such as environmental regulation considerations, operational issues, or siting
        concerns. For example, a resource with a relatively low NPVCC may also be subject to
        ongoing environmental litigation for extensive modiﬁcation requirements. In such cases,
        selection based solely on a low NPVCC value could come with increased environmental
        policy risk.

        In the 2024 IRP, OG&E did employ portfolio optimization software for expansion planning
        and production cost modeling, with the assistance of an outside consultant. The portfolio
        optimization model was used to determine the recommended mix of generation resources
        expected to achieve a projected least cost combination of generating assets to meet
        electric load along with regulatory and reliability requirements.

        Subsequent to an IRP establishing the need for capacity, procurement of resources must
        also comply with the Commission’s rules. OG&E’s 2024 All Source RFP, and 2026 All
        Source RFP, for example, are procurement processes administered consistently with rules
        for competitive procurement in OAC 165:35-34.

        OG&E’s RFP analysis follows similar processes as the IRP evaluation of resources.
        However, an RFP analysis focuses strictly on the speciﬁc projects offered in. Evaluation
        and selection of RFP resources consider all factors outlined in the RFP. Additionally, an
        RFP evaluation must also consider availability, timing, and size of the offered resource in
        order to meet the capacity needs in the least cost, least risk way. This requires careful
        consideration of the RFP scoring, resource sizing, and a wide array of execution and
        operating risks.


        3.    Description of Portfolio Optimization Software Tools
        Portfolio optimization is the process of evaluating many possible combinations of
        resources and selecting the mix that best meets deﬁned objectives while respecting
        constraints. It starts by characterizing each option of an offered resource (contract type,
        offered capacity, in-service dates, etc.) in terms of expected beneﬁts, costs, risks, and
        performance under different future conditions. These options are then combined into
        portfolios and modeled through scenarios such as demand growth, fuel price variations,
        technology performance, or regulatory changes. The core idea of portfolio optimization
        tools is that many resource combinations can be evaluated quickly. Some resources may
        perform better than others in a particular scenario but comparatively worse in a different

        scenario, so the value of a portfolio depends on how its components interact, not just on
        how each resource performs individually.


        4.    Costs
        There are a number of commercially available software tools available to conduct portfolio
        optimization that aid electric utility resource planning, such as OG&E, to make prudent
        investment decisions.

        OG&E’s preliminary annual cost estimate is up to $500,000. This estimate includes access
        for users, storage, vendor-provided data, initial training, and user support.

        These tools may differ meaningfully in their underlying approaches, modeling philosophies,
        or areas of emphasis. Differences in system architecture, workﬂow, transparency
        mechanisms, or runtime performance may inﬂuence user experience and implementation
        considerations but may not translate into materially different portfolio selection
        outcomes.

        In addition, software, regardless of platform, has limited ability to quantify or mitigate
        factors such as project development risk, execution complexity, contract terms, and
        counterparty considerations, which require separate commercial and due-diligence
        reviews.


        5.    Benefits
        The optimization step applies an objective comparison of the full range of available
        resource portfolios.

        In an IRP context, portfolio optimization can improve the quality and defensibility of
        long-term plans by systematically identifying least-cost resource portfolios over
        multi-decade horizons while satisfying planning reserve margins, reliability standards,
        environmental policies, and operational constraints. This supports more robust
        comparisons among candidate plans by (i) quantifying portfolio performance across a wide
        range of futures, (ii) revealing cost drivers and binding constraints, and (iii) highlighting
        where incremental reliability or emissions beneﬁts require material cost tradeoffs.

        Similarly, in an RFP context, portfolio optimization serves a complementary but distinct
        function by evaluating discrete bid options as candidate resources and identifying the
        combination of bids that minimizes total system cost while meeting identiﬁed needs,
        delivery timing requirements, and any portfolio-level constraints (e.g., technology diversity
        targets, siting or interconnection limitations, fuel or emissions considerations, and
        contract types). Rather than selecting projects one-by-one, optimization helps quantify

        how bids interact as a portfolio. It should be noted that utilization of a portfolio
        optimization model does not address nor reduce contract negotiation or project execution
        risk. Individual projects can face strong headwinds against completion regardless of their
        evaluated NPVCC metrics.


        6.    Conclusion
        In conclusion, several portfolio optimization software options are available that can
        effectively address quantitative analysis requirements and can be tailored to meet speciﬁc
        needs; however, they are limited in their ability to address qualitative factors.
        Implementation of portfolio optimization will require additional expenditures. OG&E is
        supportive of the usage of a portfolio optimization tool in its evaluation of projects while
        also noting that elements like project development risk, execution complexity, contractual
        terms, and counterparty dynamics often fall outside the scope of what this tool can
        meaningfully evaluate.
